name: Stress Testing Structured Credit
title: Stress Testing Structured Credit
answer: Stress testing structured credit means asking how a pool of securitised assets, and the tranches issued against it, behave when conditions turn worse than the base case. The work covers residential and commercial mortgage backed securities, collateralised loan obligations, auto and card receivables, and other asset backed deals. It sits inside fixed income and credit risk because the questions are about default timing, recovery, correlation between borrowers, and how losses travel up and down the capital structure. The output is a set of loss estimates per tranche under named scenarios, not a single number.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Stress testing structured credit means asking how a pool of securitised assets, and the tranches issued against it, behave when conditions turn worse than the base case. The work covers residential and commercial mortgage backed securities, collateralised loan obligations, auto and card receivables, and other asset backed deals. It sits inside fixed income and credit risk because the questions are about default timing, recovery, correlation between borrowers, and how losses travel up and down the capital structure. The output is a set of loss estimates per tranche under named scenarios, not a single number.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The inputs are loan level tapes, deal documents and waterfall rules, historical default and recovery series, and a scenario set that supplies paths for unemployment, house prices, interest rates and spreads. Teams run this on grid or cloud compute because a full cash flow model has to be projected month by month across thousands of paths and many deals. Common tools are Python with pandas and NumPy, R, SQL warehouses holding the loan data, and vendor platforms for cash flow and waterfall modelling. Results land in reporting layers that risk committees and regulators can read.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core is a cash flow engine that applies the deal waterfall to projected collections, so interest and principal are allocated to tranches in the documented order. Defaults and recoveries are generated from a model, often a logistic or hazard model at loan level, then correlated across the pool using a factor structure or copula. Scenarios are either historical replays, such as a severe house price decline, or hypothetical shocks agreed with the risk function. Sensitivity runs vary one assumption at a time, and backtests check whether past stress losses would have been predicted by the same setup.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Model risk management applies: documentation of assumptions, independent validation, version control, and periodic review when the portfolio or the market changes. Loan level data has privacy and contractual limits, so access is restricted and use is tied to the deal agreements. Regulators in several jurisdictions require securitisations to be stress tested and to hold capital against the results, and retention rules mean the originator usually keeps skin in the game. Provenance matters because a stress number is only as good as the tape, the scenario definition and the waterfall logic behind it, and all three need an audit trail.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more granular loan level modelling as data availability improves, and more use of machine learning for default and prepayment estimation alongside the traditional econometric models. Climate related shocks and transition risk are being folded into scenario sets for property backed deals. Faster compute and vectorised cash flow engines are shortening run times, which allows wider scenario grids and more frequent re runs. The direction is toward stress testing that is continuous rather than annual, with results feeding directly into limits, pricing and capital planning.
